items.title: Giant November Waves Threaten Surfers, Swimmers, and Spectators Along California’s Coast
items.summary:
Lifeguards along California’s coast have had their hands full over the past several days, as powerful Pacific swells stranded surfers, swept a teenager photographing the waves off rocks, and even overturned a rescue jet ski during an operation near Santa Cruz.

In San Diego alone, lifeguards conducted 175 water rescues between November 9 and 16, according to San Diego Fire-Rescue figures reported by FOX 5/KUSI .

“I’ve seen seasons start off with a bang like this, but we’ve never had this type of impact so immediate,” Ernst Bauen, operations division chief for the Central Fire District of Santa Cruz County, told Outside on November 17.

The enormous swells were generated by powerful low-pressure systems over the northeastern Pacific, where hurricane-force winds pushed waves toward the California coast, according to the National Weather Service. On November 14, forecasters predicted breaking waves of 25 to 35 feet, with occasional sets reaching 40 to 50 feet at big-wave surfing spot  Mavericks , near Half Moon Bay.

Bauen, who spent about 20 years as a rescue swimmer, said waves are reaching roads, cliffs, and beach access points earlier in the season than usual.

“The ocean is extremely dynamic, and where there used to be a safe amount of space to recreate even on the beach, those spaces are becoming fewer and further between because of the erosion along our coastline,” he said.

Rescues From Santa Cruz to San Diego

items.title: Lawmakers Move to Ban AI Data Centers on National Forests and Federal Land
items.summary:
There’s a new plan in Washington to prohibit the construction of AI data centers on public lands.

On November 11, Oregon Representative Maxine Dexter introduced the Protecting Our Public Lands from Data Centers Act , which would ban new data centers on national forests and lands managed by the U.S. Department of the Interior.

The legislation, backed by 13 Democratic cosponsors, would also require federal land sold or transferred to return to government ownership if used for a data center without congressional authorization.

“Public lands belong in public hands and Oregonians must have a say before the federal government hands over millions of acres of public land managed by the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) for data centers,” Dexter said in a November 11 press release . “These treasured lands are where people hunt, fish, hike and graze livestock. They are where wildlife habitat and our critical watersheds are protected. My bill keeps these lands safe from data centers now, and for the generations who come after us.”

The bill arrived just one day after the Interior Department published its strategic plan for fiscal years 2026 through 2030 , which outlines proposals to sell federal land to states, local governments, and tribes, while expanding energy and infrastructure development to support growing demand from data centers.

The plan drew criticism from public lands advocates, including Tracy Stone-Manning, who led the BLM under President Joe Biden and now serves as president of the Wilderness Society.

items.title: Editor’s Letter: Why Do Hard Things Outside? Our Outsiders of the Year Answer
items.summary:
“But why?”

Anyone who does hard things outside has heard it. Why climb a mountain that’s already been climbed? Why run 253 miles across a desert? To test the limits of human potential is the tidy answer. The real one, as our Outsiders of the Year show, shifts like snow on a big face: it’s different for everyone, and never quite the same twice.

This year Alex Honnold free soloed a 1,667-foot skyscraper live on Netflix, after being explained away as a brain-scan curiosity for two decades. Now 40, with two preschoolers, he fits climbing in where he can. Some days that means getting up at 2 a.m. to climb a thousand-foot granite wall to still make it home for dinner. Why bother? “In some ways, climbing is my only opportunity to feel like I’m good at something,” he tells Features Editor Frederick Dreier. Any parent who has squeezed in a run between school pickups knows the feeling.

Jim Morrison and his partner Hilaree Nelson shared a dream no one had pulled off: to climb Everest’s North Face and ski it back down. In 2022, Nelson died on Manaslu, and Morrison swore off the mountains. Then his dog started pulling him back up the trail, a little higher every day. In 2025, with Jimmy Chin filming beside him for Everest: The Other Side , Morrison skied 9,000 feet off the top of the world. At the bottom, he screamed, “That one’s for you, Hil.”

Not everyone on Everest gets to ask why. Sherpas still take the biggest risks so others can reach the top. This spring, Hillary Dawa Sherpa , a 57-year-old cook, was pushed toward the summit when his outfitter came up a guide short.…
items.t: Editor’s Letter: Why Do Hard Things Outside? Our Outsiders of the Year Answer

In the space of three years, Amflow has made a name for itself by designing versatile e-bikes that excel on mountain trails, gravel roads, and other routes that begin where the pavement ends. Now, it’s introducing a new pair of city-oriented e-bikes that exemplify the brand’s expertise in engineering, support, and safety. The UE Carbon and UE Carbon Pro might be Amflow’s first purpose-built commuter models, but they’re the culmination of everything the brand built since its inception.

Most riders spend their time in urban environments, so it makes sense that Amflow set out to design a bike that shines across the broad spectrum of daily use. The UE Carbon series builds on the brand’s history and is more than a mere concession to urban riders. This bike feels natural from the very first pedal, regardless of a rider’s size, riding style, or itinerary, and it’s tailor-made for commuting, running errands, heading on a fitness ride, and everything in between.

The UE Pro. (Photo: Amflow) 
 The foundation of the UE Carbon’s everyday adaptability is its rider-friendly design. The bike’s sleek carbon frame keeps its weight down; at 46 pounds, it’s nimble enough for navigating dense urban cores, as well as light enough for lifting onto public transport and into a storage space. A step-through design promotes an upright riding posture, which—combined with substantial adjustability and easy-to-maneuver 26-inch wheels—allows users of varying sizes to get in the saddle. items.title: How Hillary Dawa Sherpa Survived 6 Days Alone on Mount Everest
items.summary:
On May 29, a Nepali high-altitude worker named Hillary Dawa Sherpa ran out of oxygen while descending Mount Everest at the edge of the Death Zone. Days went by, and officials assumed he was dead. And then, six days after vanishing, he crawled on his hands and knees out of the Khumbu Icefall toward Base Camp, where he was rescued by camp workers.

Hillary Dawa’s improbable story of survival ignited a debate about safety and ethics on the world’s highest peak. And the 57-year-old wasn’t supposed to have been on Everest’s highest slopes in the first place.

He was originally hired to work as a seasonal cook at the Camp II setup of low-cost Nepali guiding company Himalayan Traverse Adventures. The company had just two paying clients for the 2026 season: Chris Thrall, a British ex-Royal Marine, and Mariusz Chmielewski, a plumber from Poland.

But late in the expedition, Hillary Dawa was asked to guide Thrall up the mountain, after Himalayan Traverse Adventures sent one of its experienced climbing Sherpas home.

“I was only supposed to be a cook, but they offered me 10,000 Rupees a day to climb with the clients,” Hillary Dawa told Outside . “I didn’t even want to go to Everest this year.”

Outside reached out to Himalayan Traverse Adventures but did not receive answers for this story. Hillary Dawa said company management believed Thrall was incapable of making it above Camp IV. But Thrall eventually reached the summit. Hillary Dawa and Chmielewski turned back before the top and retreated to Camp IV. On the descent, the company’s other climbing Sherpa sped ahead down the peak,…
items.t: How Hillary Dawa Sherpa Survived 6 Days Alone on Mount Everest

items.title: Astronaut Christina Koch Made History on Artemis II. But She Still Loves to Sleep in a Tent.
items.summary:
“WE ARE VERY close to being able to see Carroll Crater!” Christina Koch shouts across the campground, glancing up from her moonscope.

The NASA astronaut is bent over a small tube that looks like a telescope, attached to a tripod. A nearly full moon illuminates her curly hair, with her tent and a field of scraggly creosote bush behind her. The Big Bend National Park campsite is large enough to sleep eight people, but it’s just the two of us here tonight. Even at 10 P.M., the temperature hovers in the mid-70s. It’s already past my bedtime, but Koch and I came to the park to witness what happens in the sky after dark.

“If you look to the lower left, there’s a dark spot, almost like a mole. Carroll Crater is a little up to the left of that,” Koch says as I bend down to look through the lens, the dark splotches of the moon suddenly massive and detailed to my right eye.

Koch peers through a moonscope (Photo: Abigail Wise) 
 Koch and the other three astronauts on the 2026 Artemis II mission named Carroll Crater after colleague and mission commander Reid Wiseman’s late wife. Mission specialist Koch, Wiseman, pilot Victor Glover, and mission specialist Jeremy Hansen made history in April 2026 when they completed a ten-day-long mission around the moon, traveling a record-setting 252,757 miles from Earth, livestreaming the event, and going viral along the way. It made Koch the first woman to travel around the moon, adding another record to her list, which also includes the longest spaceflight by a woman (328 days throughout 2019 and 2020), and embarking on the first all-women…
items.t: Astronaut Christina Koch Made History on Artemis II. But She Still Loves to Sleep in a Tent.
